Beállítom A nepáli-kínai határvidéken szerdán bekövetkezett földcsuszamlás és villámárvíz után a délnyugat-kínai Tibet autonóm régióban 23 országból 261 eltűnt külföldi, köztük egy magyar után kutatnak a hatóságok – jelentette be a tibeti autonóm terület kormányzója vasárnap reggel. Az autonóm terület kormányzója azt mondta, hogy a kínai fél már tájékoztatta az érintett országok kínai nagykövetségeit és konzulátusait. A Telex kérdésre vasárnap a külügyminisztérium azt válaszolta, hogy hivatalos forrásaik jelenleg nem rendelkeznek új információval. A legfrissebb követségi jelentések továbbra is három eltűntnek nyilvánított magyar állampolgárt említenek. „A három magyar érintett kettős állampolgársággal rendelkezik. Külföldön tartózkodásuk során, közülük ketten nem a magyar okmányukkal lettek nyilvántartásba véve. Diplomatáink az illetékes hivatalokkal, az utazásszervezővel, valamint az uniós és schengeni partnerképviseletekkel folyamatosan egyeztetnek” – közölték. A tibeti autonóm terület kormányzójának közlése szerint eltűntként szerepel 104 nepáli, 49 indiai, 33 lett, 18 amerikai,15 brit, hat ausztrál, egy magyar, három német, két ír, egy spanyol, egy kazah, hat kanadai, három orosz, egy litván, három malajziai, két holland, két új-zélandi, egy portugál, egy ukrán, egy finn, két francia, két észt és négy dél-afrikai állampolgár. Hivatalos kínai adatok szerint a tibeti autonóm régióban a természeti katasztrófa 16 ember halálát okozta, 546-an pedig eltűntek. Vasárnap reggel közölt hivatalos adatok szerint Nepálban legalább 734-en haltak meg, mintegy 2498 embert pedig eltűntként tartanak nyilván. A vizsgálatok szerint nemcsak egy gleccser, hanem az alatta lévő hegyoldal leomlása együtt okozhatta a nepáli villámárvizet, ami mindent elsöpört, ami az útjába került. Az ár így nem csupán vízből állt, hanem iszap, homok, kavics és hatalmas sziklatömbök is voltak benne, ami „folyékony betonként” száguldott végig a völgyeken – mondta a Texasi Egyetem mérnökprofesszora. Ráadásul hatalmas sebességgel söpört el mindent: egy kínai kormányzati geológus közlése szerint az áradat majdnem 200 km/h-s sebességgel kezdett el száguldani lefelé, egyes helyeken elérve a több mint száz méteres magasságot. https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-thousand.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5L23h Indonesia's school meal program was launched in 2025 as a signature policy of President Prabowo Subianto Image: Muhammad Iqbal/ZUMA/picture alliance Advertisement More 1,700 people have contracted food poisoning in Indonesia over the past week after eating free school meals provided by the government as part of a new scheme. At least 725 pupils and 25 teachers at a school in Lasem on the island of Java complained that they felt unwell on Thursday morning after consuming the free lunch on Wednesday. "They had diarrhea, they were vomiting, and felt nauseous," said the school's principal. "There was a queue at the bathrooms because two of our toilets are under renovation." Earlier this week, more than 600 students in Sidoarjo, East Java, were also taken to hospital after eating free lunch meals on Tuesday. In two other cases on Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam also fell ill. Children in Sidoarjo, East Java, were taken to the regional general hospital Image: Suryanto/REUTERS One lawmaker, Charles Honoris, put the total number of food poisoning cases linked to the free school meals scheme as high as 50,000 since, citing health department data. "This is a failure of the ⁠system," he said. What has caused the food poisoning? The mass outbreaks of food poisoning have been blamed on improper food storage and late delivery of pre-cooked meals. According to the school principal in Lasem, a food taster found that some of the grilled chicken to be distributed was "slimy" and therefore put aside. "The kitchen operator said the food was cooked at 3 a.m. and it ​was eaten at noon," she reported. President Prabowo's free school meals scheme The $12.94 -billion (€11.13-billion) program, launched in January 2025, is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, intended to improve nutrition for up to 80 million children as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women. But the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, ​leadership changes and spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks. It was among the first budget items to be cut back as the Indonesian government moved to counter the economic impact of the war in the Middle East and hundreds of people took to the streets of the capital, Jakarta , last week to call for it to be scrapped entirely. How Indonesia aims to combat childhood malnutrition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "This has become a national alarm," said Ubaid Matraji, a researcher at the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network. "The government cannot continue to treat them as mere statistical figures. Behind every number there is a sick child, a panicked family, and the state's failure to guarantee safe food." The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency, ⁠which oversees the scheme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be ​handled "seriously." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Imran Khan had been briefly detained by the police on 10 October while participating in a protest in Mumbai By Meryl Sebastian BBC News Published 15 October 2026, 09:17 BST Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms. An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections. "Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday. Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court. Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting. But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest. The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic". Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na. He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992. Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly. The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade. Image source, Imran Khan/Instagram Image caption, Khan also shared a photo from inside the detention van on his Instagram page On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges. "Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement. The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India". Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest. "I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said. He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation. Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters. He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call. On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi. On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital. Vietjet launches a new twice-weekly route Hanoi-Almaty-Prague. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images Budget 2026 Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfall Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions Heather Stewart , Rowena Mason , Richard Partington and Phillip Inman Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.02 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances. Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions. In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030. Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts. “Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”. The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.” He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.” Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your pay Read more However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.” Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits. Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment. The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March. With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars. But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.” Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.” The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week. Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain. “Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.” John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share prices Read more Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further. The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.” As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs. The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn. Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.
